paras: The attempted lynching of Walter Simmons occurred on August 3, 1903, west of St. Louis, Missouri, when passengers of a derailed streetcar tried to lynch Simmons, a Black man they accused of causing the wreck. He was got away and handed to an officer, and the story ran as a short wire item the next day.
Ties piled on the St. Louis Transit Company track, two miles west of the city, derailed a Creve Coeur car and threw it down an embankment, shaking up its fifty passengers.

Simmons was found hiding near the scene; he had been put off the car ahead, and 'it is supposed' he placed the ties for revenge. The Herald and the Alexandria Gazette reported an attempt to lynch him, while the Sun said only that threats were made. Superintendent Meier ('Maler' in the Sun) got him away from the 'infuriated passengers' to Delmar and turned him over to an officer, though the Herald said 'police interfered'.
The Sun's headline said Simmons was put in jail, but no report of a charge, hearing or trial, or of action against the passengers, appears in the coverage.

The episode survives as one wire dispatch, printed on August 4 by the New York Herald, the Sun of New York and the Alexandria Gazette. The Herald headed it 'Try to Lynch a Negro' among other reports of lynching threats in Delaware and Indiana. The Sun's 'Negro Wrecks Trolley Car' and the Gazette's 'Would-be Train Wrecker Captured' treated Simmons as the culprit, though the text called the motive a supposition, and the Gazette called him 'the cowering negro'. None of the versions questioned the accusation or commented on the passengers' conduct, and no St. Louis or Black-press account was found.

Because all three versions come from one dispatch, the agreement of the fuller Gazette and Sun texts on the superintendent's role outweighs the Herald's condensed credit to the police; which of them correctly described the passengers' threat or attempt cannot be settled from the coverage.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Walter Simmons
bases: Passengers of a derailed streetcar tried to lynch (A1, A2) or threatened (A3) Walter Simmons, a Black man suspected of piling ties on the track, before a company superintendent or the police got him away.

Simmons was not killed: he was taken from the passengers and turned over to an officer (A2, A3), so this was an attempted or threatened lynching; the would-be lynchers were 'passengers' of a car carrying about fifty people, but the coverage gives no count of those who acted (A1, A2).
All three papers carry the same St. Louis wire dispatch in near-identical wording (A1, A2, A3), so they are not independent reports; no local St. Louis or Black-press account was found.

accounts.label: Wire report (fuller version)
accounts.gist: The 'infuriated passengers' attempted to lynch the 'cowering negro' (A2) or made threats (A3); Superintendent Meier got him away to Delmar and an officer. The revenge motive is given as a supposition.

framing.detail: The New York Herald ran the dispatch under 'Try to Lynch a Negro' with the subhead 'Passengers of Derailed Car Accuse Black man of Causing Wreck', among other lynching-threat items.
The Sun's headline 'Negro Wrecks Trolley Car' stated the accusation as fact, though the text called the motive a supposition.
The Alexandria Gazette headed it 'Would-be Train Wrecker Captured' and called Simmons 'the cowering negro'.

versions.value: An attempt was made to lynch him

conflicts.note: All three print the same dispatch; the Sun's wording is milder. No independent account settles which is right.

versions.value: Superintendent Meier (or 'Maler') got him away and turned him over to an officer at Delmar

conflicts.note: The two fuller versions name the company superintendent; the Herald's condensed version credits the police.
The Gazette's dateline matches its publication date; the Herald and Sun place the event on Monday, Aug. 3.
